subject: Anatomy
summary: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior forearm flexors and gives sensation to the lateral forearm. It is a key diagnostic target in elbow trauma and brachial plexus injuries. Understanding its course helps avoid iatrogenic damage during surgery.

sections.p: The musculocutaneous nerve (MCN) arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, carrying fibers from C5–C7. It supplies the biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis, and provides a lateral forearm cutaneous branch.
After branching from the lateral cord, the MCN pierces the coracobrachialis, runs between biceps and brachialis, and exits the cubital fossa to become the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
It lies anterior to the brachial artery, posterior to the median nerve, and is surrounded by the brachial veins. In the cubital fossa, it is medial to the brachial artery.
The MCN receives small arterial branches from the brachial artery and the profunda brachii. These vessels are often seen during surgical exposure.
Motor fibers to biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis; sensory fibers to lateral forearm via lateral cutaneous branch.
Facilitates elbow flexion and forearm supination. Sensory input informs proprioception and pain from the lateral forearm.

Trauma to the elbow, surgical dissection, or brachial plexus lesions can damage the MCN, leading to weak flexion and sensory loss. Common in road‑traffic accidents and obstetric brachial plexus palsy.

t.b: Assess strength of biceps and brachialis; weakness suggests MCN injury
Loss confirms MCN sensory branch involvement

sections.p: Remember the MCN is the only major nerve that exits the brachial plexus before the median nerve. In a brachial plexus injury, loss of elbow flexion with preserved wrist extension points to MCN damage.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe elbow pain with inability to flex arm
Sudden loss of sensation on lateral forearm

faq.q: What causes MCN injury in childbirth?
faq.a: Traction on the brachial plexus during shoulder dystocia can stretch the lateral cord, damaging the MCN.

faq.q: Can the MCN be repaired surgically?
faq.a: Yes, nerve grafting or direct repair is possible if identified early; outcomes improve with prompt intervention.

faq.q: How does diabetes affect the MCN?
faq.a: Diabetic neuropathy can involve the MCN, leading to chronic weakness and sensory loss, especially in poorly controlled patients.

exam: Explain the anatomical course of the musculocutaneous nerve and its clinical significance in elbow trauma.
Describe the key clinical tests to assess musculocutaneous nerve function and interpret their findings.
Discuss management steps for a patient with suspected musculocutaneous nerve injury after a road‑traffic accident.
